title: Ann And Chris

jokes.text: Leslie demanding indoor fireworks because Ann 'casually mentioned' it 3 years ago
jokes.setup: Leslie is planning a farewell party for her best friend
jokes.punchline: She tracked a throwaway comment from 3 years ago and is treating it as a binding obligation, calling a supplier to deliver indoor fireworks
jokes.explanation: Perfect Leslie characterization — her obsessive, over-the-top devotion to her friends is the show's central comedic engine. The detail of '3 years ago' makes it specific and funnier than a vague 'she mentioned once.' High character integration because this could only be Leslie.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Remember three years ago when little Tommy mentioned he liked dinosaurs? Well, I've arranged for a paleontologist to give a lecture, hired an actual animatronic T-Rex, and I'm having the caterer prepare all food in the shape of Mesozoic era creatures.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: Leslie... he was just making conversation.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: A comment is a promise, Ben. A promise I intend to keep.

jokes.text: 103 scrapbooks to capture the friendship
jokes.setup: Leslie says the friendship is 'so grand' it takes scrapbooks to document
jokes.punchline: The specific number — 103 — is the absurd escalation that lands the joke
jokes.explanation: The specificity of '103' is what sells it — not 'hundreds' or 'dozens,' but exactly 103. Pure Leslie. Economy is exceptional: three words do the entire job. Strong character integration.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: I have 103 scrapbooks documenting our friendship.

jokes.text: The pinky promise flashback launching a 5-year friendship
jokes.setup: Leslie narrates the origin of her friendship with Ann over a flashback clip
jokes.punchline: The grand, cinematic language ('That promise launched a friendship so grand') is hilariously disproportionate to the simple act of a pinky promise with a stranger
jokes.explanation: Works on two levels: the inherent sweetness of the callback to the pilot, and the comedy of Leslie treating a pinky promise like a sacred treaty. Rewatch bonus for longtime fans who recognize the pilot scene.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Come on, Harold, just one little office party. It'll be fun!

dialogue.speaker: Harold
dialogue.line: No, Leslie. I appreciate it, but I need to maintain professional boundaries.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Even if there's an ice cream sandwich?

dialogue.speaker: Harold
dialogue.line: I... well... what kind of ice cream sandwich?

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Homemade. Vanilla bean ice cream between two fresh chocolate chip cookies.

dialogue.speaker: Harold
dialogue.line: Are the cookies organic?

jokes.text: Ice cream sandwich taste test resolving the confrontation with Harold
jokes.setup: Harold from public works confronts Leslie about going over his head — a tense bureaucratic standoff
jokes.punchline: Leslie offers him a treat and he immediately softens; the scene cuts to him eating one, completely distracted from his complaint
jokes.explanation: Well-structured two-beat joke: the setup is a genuine bureaucratic conflict, the subversion is hilariously mundane (a treat). Harold's indignation is completely dissolved by food, which says something about both characters. Good scene-level economy.

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: I'm genuinely excited Ann is leaving. I mean, I'm gonna miss her and all, but mostly I'm excited.

jokes.text: 'Damn, that's really good.' / 'Right?' — Harold mid-complaint is defeated by hazelnut ice cream sandwich
jokes.setup: Harold was in the middle of a principled bureaucratic stand against Leslie
jokes.punchline: He trails off from his lecture, admits 'Damn, that's really good,' and asks about the crunch — hazelnut. He's completely disarmed.
jokes.explanation: The joke lands hardest on 'Is there a little crunch in there?' — the specificity of Harold's inquiry mid-lecture signals total capitulation. Extremely economical: the comedy is in what Harold does NOT say (his complaint) and what he does say (flavor notes). 'Ooh, right?' is a perfect button.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: Wait, what's in your box, Jerry?

dialogue.speaker: Jerry
dialogue.line: It just says 'plates' on it.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: Plates? That's it?

dialogue.speaker: Jerry
dialogue.line: Yeah, just... plates.

jokes.text: Leslie tells April she can tell she 'really cares' about Ann; April responds 'Ann's leaving town and saying painful good-byes to loved ones.'
jokes.setup: Leslie gives April a sincere compliment — that despite her teasing, April secretly cares about Ann
jokes.punchline: April's response is exactly the opposite of what a caring person would say — delivered as a flat, satisfied statement
jokes.explanation: Perfect April joke. The structure is immaculate: Leslie sets up genuine warmth, April immediately destroys it with the most April response possible. The line itself is funny in its cruelty, but the delivery context — treating Ann's departure as a victory — is quintessential April. High character integration, could only be April.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: I just made a pun and I'm very proud of it.

jokes.text: April's talking head: 'Greatest day of my life!'
jokes.setup: April has just expressed (in her twisted way) that Ann leaving is great news
jokes.punchline: Talking head of April, beaming, declaring it the greatest day of her life — pure April joy at Ann's departure
jokes.explanation: Four words, maximum laugh. Follows perfectly from the previous joke. The comedic beat of cutting to April's ecstatic talking head is a well-deployed mockumentary tool. Near-perfect economy.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: A bronzed hamburger? I appreciate the gesture, but I would prefer an edible one.

jokes.text: 'Fun pun alert.' — Chris's reaction to 'buddy boxes'
jokes.setup: Ann has just revealed 'buddy boxes' for Ann and Chris, packing mementos of their friendship
jokes.punchline: Chris excitedly flags the pun in 'buddy boxes' with 'Fun pun alert' — showing he is the kind of person who does this
jokes.explanation: 'Fun pun alert' is an absurdly specific thing to say and is pure Chris Traeger — relentlessly positive, slightly exhausting, enthusiastic about minor wordplay. High character integration. The joke is that he ANNOUNCES puns formally.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Oh my God! Oh my God! These are the Pawnee Parks Department audit spreadsheets from 1987 to 1993! Do you know how hard these are to find? These are like the holy grail of municipal documentation!

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Look at the formula work in column G. That's... that's beautiful. This is what I'm talking about. This is legendary bureaucratic work right here.

jokes.text: A bronzed hamburger as a memento from a 'turkey versus beef cook-off'
jokes.setup: Ann is giving Ben items from their friendship history
jokes.punchline: She bronzed a hamburger from a cook-off — and Ben's response ('I would have preferred a regular hamburger for eating') is the dry kicker
jokes.explanation: Two-part joke: the absurdity of bronzing a hamburger, then Ben's completely reasonable counterpoint. Ben's response is the stronger beat — it's perfectly dry and true.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: I learned about it from this guy I met at an illegal horse fighting gambling ring.

jokes.text: 2008 Indiana state audit spreadsheets — 'That was the year you went from being an auditor to a legend'
jokes.setup: Ann presents Ben with spreadsheets from a past audit as a memento
jokes.punchline: Ann calls him a 'legend' for spreadsheet work — treated with the reverence of a war hero
jokes.explanation: Plays on Ben's specific nerd-audit character history. Mildly funny — the gap between 'legend' and 'spreadsheets' is the joke. Competent but not exceptional.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Tom, I need you to not mention to Ann that we're throwing her a surprise party.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: Got it. Don't mention the surprise party to Ann.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Right. What else should you not mention?

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: Don't tell her about the ice sculpture shaped like a gazebo, the mariachi band, or that we've hired a skywriter to write 'Ann Perkins' in the sky.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: I didn't say any of those things.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: I'm just trying to cover all my bases. Also, definitely don't mention the live tiger we rented.

jokes.text: Tom gifts Ann a bottle of Snake Juice — 'I thought these were destroyed by the FDA. I did have to go to a very seedy location to find it, but now I know where to go to place a bet on horse fighting.'
jokes.setup: Tom presents Ann with a bottle of Snake Juice as a sentimental gift
jokes.punchline: The escalating revelation: the FDA destroyed them → Tom found some at a seedy location → the seedy location does horse fighting betting
jokes.explanation: This is a standout joke. Three-beat escalation that goes from nostalgic callback (Snake Juice is a fan-favorite running element) to FDA enforcement to horse fighting — each step is a surprise and each is darker than the last. 'Now I know where to go to place a bet on horse fighting' is an incredible throwaway line. Tom would absolutely end up at a horse fighting operation. High originality, strong character integration, excellent structure.

dialogue.speaker: Ann
dialogue.line: Leslie, why do you have Christmas lights, a menorah, and a giant inflatable turkey all up at the same time?

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Ann, I've solved it. I'm combining every holiday into one mega-celebration. Christmas, Hanukkah, Thanksgiving, Easter, Kwanzaa, Arbor Day, all in one party. Why limit yourself to twelve days of Christmas when you can have three hundred and sixty-five days of everything?

dialogue.speaker: Ann
dialogue.line: That's insane.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: It's efficient. We'll have a menorah Christmas tree with a turkey on top and we'll exchange gifts wrapped in wrapping paper that I designed myself with little menorahs and turkeys and candy canes and... is it working?

jokes.text: April's fake-back repeat of Leslie's instructions: 'Tell Ann about the groundbreaking, frame Ann for murder, release a deadly virus into the water supply.'
jokes.setup: Leslie tells April not to mention the groundbreaking and asks her to repeat the instruction back
jokes.punchline: April 'confirms' the instructions with increasingly unhinged additions — framing Ann for murder, releasing a deadly virus
jokes.explanation: Classic April bit perfectly executed. The structure is tight: one real instruction, then two escalating absurdities delivered in the exact same matter-of-fact tone. 'Release a deadly virus into the water supply' as the third beat is the right escalation — it goes from petty crime to bioterrorism seamlessly. And then Leslie says 'Good.' before catching herself — that beat adds another layer. Pure April, high quotability.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: Leslie's got 99 problems but a plan ain't one. She's got 150 problems and 47 contingency plans.

jokes.text: The farewell party has a New Year's Eve countdown clock AND the Easter Bunny
jokes.setup: Ann arrives at her farewell party
jokes.punchline: The party contains incongruous holiday elements including a countdown clock and the Easter Bunny — because Leslie has combined every holiday into one party
jokes.explanation: Visual gag with strong character basis: Leslie doesn't know when they'll see each other again, so she combines every holiday into one party. The Easter Bunny is the perfect incongruous detail. Rewatch bonus for background gag potential.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: I packed a bag for you! You're going to need: a scuba suit, a harmonica, seventeen pairs of mittens, a wedding dress, a fire extinguisher, and a live chicken.

dialogue.speaker: Ann
dialogue.line: Leslie, why would I need any of these things?

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Because you never know what life is going to throw at you, and I want you to be prepared for literally everything.

jokes.text: 'Ain't no party like a Leslie Knope party 'cause a Leslie Knope party is actually 30 parties.'
jokes.setup: Ann is taking in the absurdity of the multi-holiday party
jokes.punchline: Riff on 'Ain't no party like a TLC party' — the twist being that Leslie's parties are literally multiple parties collapsed into one
jokes.explanation: Good line that earns its cultural reference by actually twisting it — '30 parties' is specific and correct. The pun structure works. Fairly quotable.

dialogue.speaker: Chris
dialogue.line: A gift card to Pots and Pans? That's amazing! I love cooking! Well, I mean, I love the idea of cooking. I've never actually done it. But this is great! I can finally buy that one pot I've always wanted. Or maybe a pan. Probably just one or the other though, given the card's limit.

jokes.text: 'Knope, you have out-Knoped yourself.'
jokes.setup: Harold is at the party and observing Leslie's extreme effort
jokes.punchline: The meta construction of 'out-Knoped yourself' — using her name as both verb and standard
jokes.explanation: A tight, economical line. Using a character's surname as a verb is a reliable comedic device, and it works here because 'Knoped' captures something real about Leslie's character. The slight surprise that Harold says it is an added bonus.

dialogue.speaker: Chris
dialogue.line: You know what? I'm actually excited about this. I've been doing some research on nutritional yeast-based desserts, and I think we could really make something special here. Sure, it might not sound appetizing to most people, but I genuinely believe that once everyone tries a low-sodium, sugar-free, gluten-free mousse made with activated charcoal and stevia, they're going to understand what real dessert is all about.

jokes.text: April tries to speed Ann out the door: 'Ann, you probably wanna head to Michigan forever, so I snuck into your house and packed a bag for you. Bye.'
jokes.setup: The party is ongoing; April wants Ann gone
jokes.punchline: April snuck into Ann's house and packed her bag as a 'gift' to expedite her departure — delivered with complete casual sincerity
jokes.explanation: Pure April — the act of breaking into someone's house is presented as a thoughtful gesture. 'Bye.' as the button is perfect economy. The character integration is excellent; April's brand of dark helpfulness is very specific.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: I got him a gift card to Chipotle. For twenty dollars.

jokes.text: The bag April packed contains 'a bunch of bras and knives. And loose onions.'
jokes.setup: Ann opens the bag April packed for her emergency departure
jokes.punchline: The contents — bras, knives, and loose onions — are a perfect April inventory of random, slightly threatening items
jokes.explanation: This is one of the episode's best jokes. 'Bras and knives' is already a perfectly April combination — functional but vaguely threatening — and then 'And loose onions' is the escalating absurdist kicker that elevates it. The specificity of 'loose' is crucial; a bag of onions would be less funny. Three-item list with a great third beat. High originality and character integration.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: What about a gift certificate to a nice restaurant? Or maybe some cologne? Oh, or a leather jacket!

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: Dude, you're just describing yourself.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: What? No, I'm not.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: Tom, you literally just listed cologne, a leather jacket, and expensive dinners. Those are your three main personality traits.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: ...I need to reevaluate some things.

jokes.text: The group's farewell gift to Chris: a gift card from 'Pots and Pans' — 'that card's for three pans'
jokes.setup: The gang is pooling their gift ideas for Chris's farewell; they've clearly put in minimal effort
jokes.punchline: The gift is a modest gift card for a generic home store — and it's only worth three pans
jokes.explanation: Sets up the running gag of the group's terrible gifts for Chris. Functional joke — the contrast between Chris's elaborate buddy boxes and a three-pan gift card is the setup for a longer bit. Works more as setup than punchline.

dialogue.speaker: Donna
dialogue.line: I'm going to dominate the Pawnee dating scene.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: Well, I mean, I've got a pretty good track record with the ladies—

dialogue.speaker: Donna
dialogue.line: Tom, no.

jokes.text: Carob cookies and berries are Chris's corner of the party — and he's genuinely delighted by it
jokes.setup: Tom mentions that the party has 'one corner for you' (Chris) with carob cookies and berries
jokes.punchline: Chris responds 'Carob cookies and berries are literally my favorite dessert alternative' — his health obsession means the insulting consolation prize is actually perfect for him
jokes.explanation: Good character joke — Tom's diminishment lands as a compliment because of Chris's specific character traits. The irony is earned through consistent characterization. 'Dessert alternative' is a great word choice.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: I'm not banned from the Ice Rink. I just choose not to go there anymore.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: There's a sign that says 'Leslie Knope is banned.'

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: That could apply to anyone named Leslie Knope.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: It has your picture on it.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: It could be anyone with my face.

jokes.text: 'I also shook his hand. Twice. Anything more than that would be excessive.'
jokes.setup: Ben says he feels bad for only getting Chris a gift card; Tom admits his contribution was shaking Chris's hand
jokes.punchline: Two handshakes, delivered with total confidence that this is proportionate — and the defensive 'Anything more than that would be excessive' seals it
jokes.explanation: Excellent Tom joke. His self-justifying logic — two handshakes is the right amount — is perfectly economical and perfectly in character. The defensive follow-up ('Anything more would be excessive') is the crucial second beat. Tom's lazy gift-giving is well-established; this is an original and sharp expression of it.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: What the—Malia and Sasha! I mean, I love them both equally.

jokes.text: 'I say we start with the three C's — cashmere, concert tickets, caboodles of cash.'
jokes.setup: The group is brainstorming a better gift for Chris
jokes.punchline: Tom's 'three C's' are three things he himself would want, presented as universal gift wisdom — and 'caboodles of cash' is specifically Tom-speak
jokes.explanation: Tom's gift suggestions reveal only his own desires. 'Caboodles of cash' is a Tom Haverford phrase (the alliteration, the slightly archaic word 'caboodles'). Competent Tom character comedy.

dialogue.speaker: Ann
dialogue.line: Okay Chris, for your mood, you need to take a B12 supplement, do 20 minutes of cardio, eat a salad with at least seven different vegetables, get exactly eight hours of sleep, meditate for ten minutes, drink half your body weight in water, take a probiotic, do some light stretching, and wear sunscreen even though it's cloudy.

jokes.text: 'I feel like those are perfect gifts for you.' / 'Those are perfect gifts for anyone.'
jokes.setup: Ben correctly calls out that Tom's suggestions are for himself
jokes.punchline: Tom disagrees with total sincerity — he genuinely believes his tastes are universal
jokes.explanation: Clean two-line exchange. Tom's obliviousness to his own narcissism is the joke — and the counter-assertion with 'anyone' is a good button. Economy is strong.

dialogue.speaker: Ann
dialogue.line: Chris went to get some coffee. He said something about wanting to listen to his 'jams' on the way.

dialogue.speaker: Chris
dialogue.line: Hey everyone! I know some of you think my music taste is a little... unconventional. But you know what? I see that as a positive! It means I'm not afraid to be myself and explore new sonic landscapes. Plus, the energy from these tracks really helps me maintain my optimal heart rate during my morning jog. It's a win-win!

jokes.text: 'Ugh, I wish you guys were Donna!'
jokes.setup: The brainstorming session is going nowhere
jokes.punchline: Tom's exasperated cry that he wishes his colleagues were Donna — a statement of affection for Donna disguised as an insult to everyone else
jokes.explanation: Four words that reveal Tom's character hierarchy. Works because it's simultaneously an insult to Ben and the others and a genuine compliment to Donna. Economy is strong.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: Wait, we dated? For like what, a few months?

dialogue.speaker: Ann
dialogue.line: Two years, Andy. Two years.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: Right, right. That's what I said. Anyway, I hope you're happy in... Arizona.

dialogue.speaker: Ann
dialogue.line: Michigan. I'm moving to Michigan.

jokes.text: Donna: 'I'm 100% sure that I will not meet another Donna Meagle in Michigan.'
jokes.setup: Donna is saying goodbye to Ann
jokes.punchline: Donna's farewell is entirely about Donna — framing the loss of herself as Ann's primary problem in Michigan
jokes.explanation: Perfectly Donna — narcissistic but also probably correct. The self-referential framing as a comfort ('don't worry about leaving me, worry about LOSING me') is her specific character register.

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: I have a confession to make. I'm actually really upset about the groundbreaking complications.

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: My real fear is that Ann might not leave.

jokes.text: Donna: 'But now that you're officially out of the dating pool, you know I'm gonna run this town, right?' / Ann: 'Oh. Oh, yeah, you do not wanna go down that road. Trust me, I tried.'
jokes.setup: Donna says with Ann gone she'll run the Pawnee dating scene
jokes.punchline: Ann's warning — 'you do not wanna go down that road, trust me, I tried' — is an honest assessment of Pawnee's dating pool being terrible, delivered with genuine trauma
jokes.explanation: References Ann's legendarily bad dating history (the entire run of the show). Solid character comedy but relies on prior knowledge to fully land.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: Ann, you're my best friend. I want you to know that no matter what happens, I will always be there for you.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: I can see our future together. We're older now, gray hair, sitting on a porch. Chris is dead.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: We're poor. I'm asking you for money. You say no. I cry a little.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: But we're together, and that's what matters.

jokes.text: Ron: 'I've been mostly focused on these ribs. By the way, you're out of Easter ham and Thanksgiving turkey.'
jokes.setup: Ben asks Ron if he's seen April; Ron was presumably nearby when a 'nice moment' might have occurred
jokes.punchline: Ron has been exclusively focused on eating meat from the multi-holiday party — and delivers an inventory update as if it's the relevant information
jokes.explanation: Perfect Ron joke. He's oblivious to everything except meat, and his report on the meat inventory is delivered as genuinely useful information. The callback to the multi-holiday party (Easter ham and Thanksgiving turkey in the same sentence) adds a layer. High character integration.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: I'm not one for goodbyes, but I want you to know that working with you has been... adequate. You've done some things that I didn't actively oppose, and that's saying something. I respect your work ethic, even if most of your ideas are mediocre. You're a fine employee, and I mean that in the most lukewarm way possible.

jokes.text: The fence has a sign reading 'No trespassing — especially Leslie Knope'
jokes.setup: Leslie learns the public works department blocked the lot with a padlock
jokes.punchline: The sign specifically names Leslie Knope — she is such a known quantity that they added a personal callout to a generic trespassing sign
jokes.explanation: Great character joke — Leslie's reputation for bureaucratic end-runs is so established that someone preemptively added her name to a legal sign. The specificity ('especially') is the right word.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: I've contributed my gift: I wrote my name on this rock. It's a paperweight.

jokes.text: 'Well, Leslie Knope is a very common name. There's a professor in Copenhagen named Leslie Knope. They probably mean him.'
jokes.setup: Ben tells Leslie there's a picture of her on the sign
jokes.punchline: Leslie's desperate, increasingly specific rationalizations — inventing a male professor in Copenhagen — as her denial escalates
jokes.explanation: Leslie's denial escalates perfectly — 'common name' is one thing, but inventing a specific male professor in a specific European city is committed absurdism. 'They probably mean him' as a button is great. Ben's straight-man follow-up ('Do they mean the professor?') lands perfectly too.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: Sweetums!

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: What? It just came out.

jokes.text: 'Holy mother of Malia! And Sasha. I love them both equally.'
jokes.setup: Leslie reacts to the news about the security guards blocking the lot
jokes.punchline: Leslie's exclamation invokes the Obama daughters — and then immediately corrects herself to include Sasha so as not to show favoritism
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's standout jokes. Leslie's worship of the Obama family is deep established characterization, but the joke's genius is the immediate self-correction — she's so committed to treating the Obama daughters fairly that she adds Sasha as a moral obligation mid-exclamation. The structure is perfect: exclamation, correction, justification. Highly quotable and very specific to Leslie.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: I can grant your wishes, within reason. I'm not a genie. I'm a mid-level bureaucrat with a can-do attitude and a laminating machine.

jokes.text: Leslie can't watch Julie Andrews before bedtime because it gets her 'too hyper'
jokes.setup: Ben and Chris are exchanging spousal care tips as their partners leave
jokes.punchline: Ben's care instruction reveals Leslie is hyper-stimulated by Julie Andrews movies — a childlike quality delivered as a serious medical warning
jokes.explanation: Good character joke — Leslie's childlike enthusiasm is a core trait, and imagining her bouncing off the walls after a Julie Andrews film is completely believable. The framing as a care tip (like a babysitting instruction) adds a layer.

dialogue.speaker: Harold
dialogue.line: You want me to unblock your project? Fine. But I want free soda back in the break room.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: That's it? That's your demand?

dialogue.speaker: Harold
dialogue.line: You took away my free soda, Leslie. You took away my joy.

jokes.text: Chia seeds stuffed into a fig calms Chris when cranky around noon
jokes.setup: Ben and Chris are trading spousal care instructions
jokes.punchline: Chris's care is so specific and health-food-coded — 'stuff some chia seeds into a fig' — that it plays as both plausible and absurd
jokes.explanation: Solid Chris character joke — his health-food obsession is well-captured in 'chia seeds into a fig.' Not as sharp as the Julie Andrews line but works in the paired structure.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: I'm terrified. What if Kathryn hates me? What if she thinks I'm a terrible person?

dialogue.speaker: Ann
dialogue.line: Leslie, you're one of the best people I know. Anyone who knows you knows that.

jokes.text: 'Wow, we really picked some intense people to spend our lives with, huh?'
jokes.setup: Ben and Ann have just exchanged the Julie Andrews rule and the chia-seed-in-fig tip
jokes.punchline: The quiet mutual acknowledgment that Leslie and Chris are a lot — delivered with warm resignation
jokes.explanation: A solid straight-man moment shared between two of the show's normal characters. Works as a button on the exchange but isn't a standout joke. The warmth underneath makes it land emotionally as much as comedically.

dialogue.speaker: Kathryn
dialogue.line: Oh, you want my help? That's adorable. Leslie, your enthusiasm is like a golden retriever that learned to use a megaphone. And Ann, honey, your face has all the character of a mayonnaise sandwich.

jokes.text: Chris dances to 'One Headlight' by the Wallflowers; Ann tells him it's not 'dancing' music; Chris says 'Not with that attitude'
jokes.setup: Ben asks where Chris is; Ann explains why he's not here
jokes.punchline: 'Not with that attitude' — Chris's relentless positivity applied to making a sad 90s alt-rock song into dance music
jokes.explanation: Excellent Chris joke. 'One Headlight' is specifically not a dancing song — it's a mournful grunge/alternative track — which makes the choice pointed. And 'Not with that attitude' is perfectly Chris: his optimism applied to literally anything. High character integration, highly quotable.

dialogue.speaker: Kathryn
dialogue.line: You're nothing but a walking participation trophy.

dialogue.speaker: Ann
dialogue.line: Oh yeah? Well I'm pregnant, and I will hurt you.

jokes.text: Andy: 'Dude, Ann, you know what I just remembered? We used to date. Yeah, we lived together for two years. I know, it's crazy, right? Anyways, you're the best. Have fun in Mexico.'
jokes.setup: Andy has a realization he wants to share with Ann at her farewell party
jokes.punchline: Andy barely remembers they dated and lived together for two years — treats it as a fun trivia fact — and then sends her off to the wrong country
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's best jokes and possibly the best in the episode. Multiple layers: (1) Andy barely remembers a two-year relationship, (2) he treats this revelation as charming small talk, (3) 'I know, it's crazy, right?' — he's the one who's surprised, (4) 'Anyways, you're the best' — the emotional reset to complete obliviousness, (5) 'Have fun in Mexico' — she's moving to Michigan, not Mexico. Each element compounds. Pure Andy, could not be any other character. Exceptional character integration and structure.

dialogue.speaker: Detlef
dialogue.line: I'm so tired of being typecast as a basketball player. People see me and that's all they think about.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Detlef, you're literally drinking a cocktail called 'The Slam Dunk' that comes in a glass shaped like a basketball hoop.

jokes.text: April is 'scared that this means Ann won't really leave' — she's crying tears of worry that the plan will fail
jokes.setup: Ann asks if April is okay, apparently seeing genuine distress
jokes.punchline: April reveals she's scared not because Ann is leaving, but because she's scared Ann WON'T leave
jokes.explanation: Good misdirection — we expect a crack in April's armor, a moment of genuine feeling. Instead she has genuine feeling about Ann NOT leaving. The subversion of the expected emotional beat is well-executed.

dialogue.speaker: Perd
dialogue.line: I'm a journalist. I have to maintain my integrity. I cannot be swayed by personal appeals or—

dialogue.speaker: Ann
dialogue.line: Perd, could you please not run that story?

dialogue.speaker: Perd
dialogue.line: Consider it killed.

jokes.text: Tom's farewell speech to Ann: 'I'm deleting you from my phone. You're finally free of my animal magnetism.'
jokes.setup: Tom gives Ann a going-away present
jokes.punchline: His 'gift' is deleting her contact — framed as liberating her from his attractiveness
jokes.explanation: 'Animal magnetism' is a great Tom Haverford phrase — his self-mythology in two words. Framing a phone deletion as a gift is perfectly Tom: self-involved but also oddly sweet.

dialogue.speaker: Ann
dialogue.line: So I went on a date with Perd.

dialogue.speaker: Perd
dialogue.line: Ann, I am here to inform you that I have developed romantic feelings for you, which I will now announce on live television.

jokes.text: Tom's extended fantasy: When they're both old and Chris is dead, he'll see Ann at his mega club and let her in the back door because she's 'too old'
jokes.setup: Tom describes a scenario where they reconnect in the future
jokes.punchline: The scenario escalates to include Chris being dead, Tom having a bouncer/bodyguard, and letting Ann in through the back because she'd be too old for the club — presented as deeply generous
jokes.explanation: Dark and Tom-specific — the casual inclusion of 'Chris is dead' is a great dark beat. The 'bouncer/bodyguard' fusion and the back-door 'generosity' add layers. A bit long but the escalation earns it. Ann's 'That's very generous' is the perfect straight-man button.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: Okay, here's what we do. We tell them that the gifts were delayed in shipping, but they're coming. They're coming soon. Real soon.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: And then, when they ask about it in a few weeks, we say there was a problem at the warehouse. A small fire. Nothing major, but it set us back.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: Then we tell them the replacement gifts are stuck in customs in Singapore. Which, by the way, is real. That's a real place.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: And then, after like two months, we just show up with some really nice gifts that we definitely spent money on, and they'll be so grateful, they won't even care.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: Plus, we can write off the gifts as a charitable donation, which means my taxes go down. It's foolproof.

jokes.text: Ann: 'That's very generous.' Tom: 'Stay golden, sweetheart.' Ann: 'I'm gonna miss you too, Tom.'
jokes.setup: Tom finishes his elaborate, self-centered farewell fantasy
jokes.punchline: Ann's sincere 'That's very generous' + 'I'm gonna miss you too, Tom' — she received this speech as genuine affection, which is the correct read of Tom
jokes.explanation: The emotional button on Tom's bit. Works because it's both funny and genuinely warm — Ann sees through Tom's nonsense to the real affection underneath.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: Ask not what your country can do for you, ask what you can do for your country.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: That's from Family Guy.

jokes.text: Ron's farewell to Ann: 'I have enjoyed parts of our time together.'
jokes.setup: Ron gives Ann a farewell
jokes.punchline: 'Parts' — Ron can't bring himself to say he enjoyed all of their time together, so he qualifies with the minimum honest claim
jokes.explanation: Near-perfect Ron Swanson joke. Six words. 'Parts' is the entire joke — it conveys that he DOES care but cannot bring himself to overclaim. The word choice is surgically precise. In context it's also genuinely touching because coming from Ron, this IS a glowing review. Ann's response ('Oh, God, Ron') is the perfect reaction. One of the most economical character jokes in the episode.

dialogue.speaker: Chris
dialogue.line: Ask not what your country can do for you, ask what you can do for your country.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: That's from Family Guy.

jokes.text: Ron's gift: a piece of paper that says 'Ron.'
jokes.setup: Ron is asked for his gift contribution for Chris
jokes.punchline: Ron holds up a piece of paper that simply says 'Ron' — his name, presented as a complete gift
jokes.explanation: Absurdist perfection in one prop. Ron has contributed his name — and nothing else — as a gift. It's both completely lazy and completely Ron (a man of few words). The visual of him presenting a piece of paper that says 'Ron' is a great sight gag. Economy is absolute maximum.

dialogue.speaker: Chris
dialogue.line: You know, I've been thinking about our friendship, and I realized something. We've been through so much together. And even when things get tough, we always have each other. That's what really matters.

dialogue.speaker: Chris
dialogue.line: So I got you this gift to show you how much you mean to me.

dialogue.speaker: Chris
dialogue.line: It's... well, it's empty. But that's kind of the point. It's empty because our friendship is so full.

jokes.text: Chris opens the gift bag: 'Some assorted items. And...some pieces of paper. Boom, nailed it.'
jokes.setup: The group presents Chris with their assembled 'gift bag' of terrible contributions
jokes.punchline: Ben's narration of the contents ('assorted items,' 'pieces of paper') exposes their worthlessness, capped with 'Boom, nailed it' — forced self-congratulation
jokes.explanation: Good payoff to the gift-gathering running gag. 'Assorted items' and 'pieces of paper' are the right self-aware descriptions of their failure. 'Boom, nailed it' is Ben abandoning all pretense — and works because Ben is usually more self-aware than this.

dialogue.speaker: Harold
dialogue.line: You two are a couple of pains in the ass.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Well, Harold, I prefer to think of it as we're a couple of asses that cause pain. Which is actually a compliment, because it means we're effective. And effectiveness is something to be proud of.

jokes.text: There is a pilgrim line-dancing with a box of candies at the party
jokes.setup: Chris is complimenting the party to Leslie
jokes.punchline: Chris's specific observation — a pilgrim line dancing with a box of candies — is a perfect window into the party's absurdity
jokes.explanation: Pilgrim = Thanksgiving, candies = Halloween/Christmas, line dancing is just chaos. The specificity of this background detail is well-chosen. Rewatch bonus for the visual of it actually being there.

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: If you want to deal with raccoons, you have to think like a raccoon. They're trash pandas - they're smart, they're vicious, and they'll steal your wallet. So you need to set traps, but not regular traps. You need to use psychology. Leave out shiny objects mixed with spoiled food, play recordings of other raccoons fighting, and whatever you do, never make eye contact because that's a sign of dominance and they will attack.

jokes.text: Leslie's genius in getting the key: 'Just think of us as your genies who can give you anything you want. Nothing gross.'
jokes.setup: Leslie is trying to negotiate with Harold for the key
jokes.punchline: 'Nothing gross.' — Leslie immediately limits the genie offer, which implies the most obvious wish is gross
jokes.explanation: The 'nothing gross' addition is the joke — it reveals what Leslie expects people to wish for from attractive women offering wishes. Quick and well-placed.

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: If a raccoon ever approaches you, you need to puff up your body to make yourself look bigger, like a puffer fish. Then you hiss really loud and back away slowly. They hate that.

jokes.text: Harold's demand: free soda. Specifically the Sweetums brand that Kathryn Pinewood discontinued.
jokes.setup: Harold has leverage; Leslie says to name his price for the key
jokes.punchline: His demand is not power, money, or glory — it's free soda. 'Super fizzy fruity pop.'
jokes.explanation: Good misdirection — the bureaucratic standoff resolves into a request for fizzy soda. 'Super fizzy fruity pop' is a charmingly childish way to describe soda. Harold's pettiness is satisfying.

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: At least you'll get to experience nature. The wolverines there are very aggressive.

jokes.text: Ann's farewell to April: April summarizes what Ann was going to say ('Yeah, you saw a lot of potential in me...blah blah blah, bye.') before Ann can say it
jokes.setup: Ann is beginning a heartfelt goodbye speech to April
jokes.punchline: April speed-runs the expected emotional content, summarizing it as 'blah blah blah, bye' — then acknowledges it's accurate
jokes.explanation: Excellent April joke — she pre-empts the emotional moment by cataloging it as cliché, then the reveal that she's essentially correct ('That is remarkably close to what I was going to say') makes it both funny and actually touching. The self-awareness is perfectly April without breaking character.

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: I love you.

dialogue.speaker: Ann
dialogue.line: I'm not going to make you say it again, am I?

jokes.text: April quietly adds: 'Also, I'm proud of you.'
jokes.setup: April has just dismissed the emotional farewell as 'blah blah blah'
jokes.punchline: After a beat, she quietly adds a sincere compliment — the contrast with her dismissiveness makes it land harder
jokes.explanation: The comedic-emotional pivot that makes the previous joke great. The timing — separated by a scene break, quietly delivered — is what elevates it. It's funny because it breaks April's pattern but also deeply in character because she would ONLY allow herself this much sincerity. Rewatch bonus because knowing it's coming makes the setup even funnier.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: I made a box. It has four sides, a bottom, and a top. The wood is from a hickory tree that fell in my backyard. I let it season for three years before milling it myself with a hand plane. The joinery is mortise and tenon, which I cut with a chisel and mallet. Each joint is reinforced with hide glue, which I rendered from horse hooves. The finish is linseed oil, applied by hand in seven coats. The box measures 14 and 7/16 inches by 9 and 3/8 inches by 6 and 1/2 inches, with a tolerance of 1/32 of an inch. It holds things.

jokes.text: Donna grabs Ann's butt. Ann: 'Donna, are you grabbing my butt?' Donna: 'Can you blame me?' Ann: 'No!'
jokes.setup: Donna and Ann are having a goodbye moment
jokes.punchline: Donna has grabbed Ann's butt; when called out, her defense ('Can you blame me?') is an appeal to Ann's objective attractiveness — and Ann's 'No!' concedes the point
jokes.explanation: Three-line exchange that works perfectly. Donna's defense is so matter-of-fact that it becomes reasonable, and Ann's concession ('No!') is the right button. Very Donna.

dialogue.speaker: Jerry
dialogue.line: Those are my initials. Garry, Jerry, Larry, Garry, Gergich.

dialogue.speaker: Jerry
dialogue.line: My parents couldn't decide on a name, so they just kept changing it. I've been burned so many times, I figured I'd just use all of them.

jokes.text: Kathryn Pinewood: 'Sorry, can't help you ladies. I don't have time for disgraced former politicians and unmarried preggos.'
jokes.setup: Leslie and Ann approach Kathryn Pinewood for help getting the sodas back
jokes.punchline: Pinewood's dismissal is hilariously specific and rude — 'disgraced former politicians' (Leslie's recall) and 'unmarried preggos' (Ann) — delivered as polite declination
jokes.explanation: Pinewood is a recurring antagonist and her rudeness is always specific and targeted. 'Unmarried preggos' is a specifically awful thing to say which makes it funnier. The specificity of each insult (tied to each character's actual circumstances) elevates it above generic villainy.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: Those better not be tears on that wood. Moisture is the enemy of fine craftsmanship.

jokes.text: Leslie: 'Oh, Kathryn, always a delight.'
jokes.setup: Pinewood has just been extremely rude to both of them
jokes.punchline: Leslie's response is a complete inversion — 'always a delight' for someone who is never a delight
jokes.explanation: Standard sarcasm — not particularly original but functional. Works as a character moment (Leslie being polite under fire) more than as a standalone joke.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: You taught me that it's okay to wear unflattering clothing if it makes you happy.

dialogue.speaker: Ann
dialogue.line: I did not teach you that.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: You're living it every day.

jokes.text: Pregnant Ann puts Kathryn Pinewood in a headlock: 'I'm pregnant and I have you in a headlock. And if you try to fight back, I will sue you.'
jokes.setup: Leslie is being pushed away from Pinewood and losing the negotiation
jokes.punchline: Ann steps in with a physical headlock and legal threat — a pregnant woman deploying her pregnancy as both a physical and legal weapon
jokes.explanation: Excellent joke. The surprise of Ann (generally the sane one) putting someone in a headlock is great, but the specific genius is using her pregnancy as leverage in two ways simultaneously: (1) physically — you can't fight a pregnant woman (2) legally — if you do, I'll sue. 'I'm pregnant and I have you in a headlock' is a great construction. Highly quotable.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Ann, you taught me so much. You taught me about friendship, about loyalty, about being a good person. You taught me that it's okay to be yourself, even when the world tells you to be someone else. You taught me about compassion and kindness and standing up for what's right. And most importantly, Ann, you taught me that a woman should never, ever wear a tulip skirt.

jokes.text: The Sweetums drink is called 'Sweetums Dunktastic Three-Point B-Ball Blast' with the slogan 'It's all about basketball'
jokes.setup: Ron says he was approached to be a spokesman for Sweetums's new sports drink
jokes.punchline: The product name and slogan are maximally on-the-nose — as if a sports drink was named and marketed by someone who had just learned what basketball is
jokes.explanation: Classic Parks and Rec product comedy — Sweetums consistently produces absurd food/drink items. 'It's all about basketball' as a slogan for a drink is perfectly stupid. Ron's complaint ('when is this town gonna realize I'm more than a former basketball star?') while refusing to endorse a basketball drink is also a nice character beat.

dialogue.speaker: Ann
dialogue.line: Well, I guess now that the park is finished, you don't need me anymore. Our friendship was just transactional.

jokes.text: Perd: 'Well, the story of that appeal is it was heartfelt. And in response to that appeal, I respond: Okay.'
jokes.setup: Leslie makes a sincere 'for old time's sake' appeal to Perd
jokes.punchline: Perd narrates his own decision-making process in the third person using his news anchor voice — 'The story of that appeal is it was heartfelt'
jokes.explanation: Perd narrating his own emotional response as if it's breaking news is perfect. 'In response to that appeal, I respond: Okay' is the ideal Perd sentence — over-structured, recursive, and ending in an anticlimax. Strong character integration.

dialogue.speaker: Ann
dialogue.line: Well, I guess our friendship is just a series of transactions at this point.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: What? No! Ann, you're my best friend.

dialogue.speaker: Ann
dialogue.line: Really? Because I'm pretty sure you only hang out with me when you need something.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: That is not true! I... okay, fine. But I'm working on it.

jokes.text: Revelation: Ann went on a date with Perd Hapley during her 'explore my freedom as a single woman' phase
jokes.setup: Leslie is confused about why Perd agreed 'for old time's sake'
jokes.punchline: Ann reveals she went on a date with Perd — and he ended the evening saying 'I am going to kiss you now by putting my mouth on your mouth' — then she ran away
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's biggest laughs. The reveal that Ann dated Perd is absurd on its own, but Perd's specific declaration — 'I am going to kiss you now by putting my mouth on your mouth' — is a perfect, horrifying example of Perd-speak applied to romance. 'And then I ran away' as the kicker is exactly right. High originality, excellent structure, and highly quotable.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: Shotgun!

dialogue.speaker: Jerry
dialogue.line: Actually, I called it first.

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: Nobody called anything. We're taking two cars.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: Wait, why are we taking two cars?

dialogue.speaker: Donna
dialogue.line: Because apparently there's a rule now that you have to call shotgun before you even know where you're going.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: This is ridiculous. In my day, the strongest person just sat wherever they wanted.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Actually, according to the official shotgun rules I've established, you need to call it within five minutes of entering the parking lot, and only if you're wearing closed-toe shoes.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: That's insane.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: It's in the handbook I printed for everyone.

dialogue.speaker: Ann
dialogue.line: You made a handbook about car seating?

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: A 40-page handbook. And as of today, shotgun is actually illegal.

dialogue.speaker: Everyone
dialogue.line: What?

jokes.text: Tom's scheme: Tell Chris they were robbed at gunpoint, then Chris feels bad and buys THEM gifts. 'Next thing you know, Tommy's got a new watch.'
jokes.setup: Ben suggests telling Chris the truth about the bad gifts
jokes.punchline: Tom proposes an elaborate con where they victimize themselves and convert Chris's sympathy into gifts for Tom specifically — ending in 'Tommy's got a new watch'
jokes.explanation: Tom's plan being specifically designed so that HE gets a new watch, rather than getting Chris anything, is perfectly Tom. 'Tommy's got a new watch' as the end goal of an elaborate sympathy con is a great specificity. The logic is internally consistent and deeply selfish.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: Shotgun!

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: Shotgun!

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: Shotgun!

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Shotgun!

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: Shotgun!

dialogue.speaker: Donna
dialogue.line: Shotgun!

dialogue.speaker: Jerry
dialogue.line: Shotgun!

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: I'm driving.

jokes.text: 'I shook the man's hand. Twice.' (repeated)
jokes.setup: Discussion of whether their gifts for Chris are sufficient
jokes.punchline: Tom repeats his earlier defense of the double handshake as a complete gift
jokes.explanation: Running gag payoff — the repetition confirms this is Tom's sincere position, not a one-off. The callback earns a laugh because we recognize it's become his mantra.

jokes.text: Jerry holds up an Abraham Lincoln hat and misattributes 'Ask not what your country can do for you' to Abraham Lincoln — 'From Family Guy, right?'
jokes.setup: Jerry triumphantly returns from the President's Day booth with a gift
jokes.punchline: Jerry misattributes JFK's quote to Lincoln (already wrong), then compounds it by attributing it to Family Guy
jokes.explanation: Double error escalation: misattributing JFK to Lincoln is already a Jerry mistake, but 'From Family Guy, right?' is a second, more spectacular wrong turn. The ascending wrongness is well-structured. Pure Jerry — enthusiastic, wrong, and proud.

jokes.text: Ben and Tom confess to Chris: 'We feel bad because you got us such thoughtful gifts and we got you three pans and a bag of nothing.'
jokes.setup: Ben and Tom decide to tell Chris the truth about the inadequate gifts
jokes.punchline: 'A bag of nothing' is the honest and perfect summary of what they assembled for Chris
jokes.explanation: 'A bag of nothing' is the right name for what they gave him — honest, self-aware, and the correct conclusion to the running gag. Works as a closing beat on the thread.

jokes.text: Chris: 'Just the fact that you feel bad about your bag of nothing proves that.'
jokes.setup: Ben and Tom have just confessed the lameness of their gifts
jokes.punchline: Chris reframes the 'bag of nothing' as evidence of their good character — his relentless positivity turns their failure into a virtue
jokes.explanation: Perfect Chris — his optimism is so extreme that a bag of nothing becomes meaningful through the lens of guilt. 'Bag of nothing' being picked up and used seriously is a good running-word callback.

jokes.text: Leslie: 'Harold, your tiny brain could not understand this, but that is the best compliment you could ever give the two women standing in front of you.'
jokes.setup: Harold calls them 'a couple of real pains in the ass'
jokes.punchline: Leslie interprets his insult as the highest compliment — and specifically notes his brain is too small to understand why
jokes.explanation: Leslie reframing bureaucratic obstruction as a badge of honor is consistent with her character. The 'tiny brain' addition is the right escalation — she's both accepting the compliment and insulting him simultaneously.

jokes.text: April's raccoon advice: 'You have to hiss really loud and stomp your feet... and if one comes close, make yourself really large like a puffer fish.'
jokes.setup: April is apparently doing something with raccoons on the Sullivan Street lot
jokes.punchline: April's raccoon-deterrence advice is specific, confident, and delivered as if she has practiced this extensively
jokes.explanation: April's affinity for dark, animal, slightly feral things is well-established. 'Make yourself really large like a puffer fish' is a good specific detail. Competent character comedy.

jokes.text: Ann: 'That is one thing I will not miss.' / Leslie: 'Well, Michigan has wolverines. Maybe they'll eat your toes.'
jokes.setup: Ann says she won't miss Pawnee raccoons
jokes.punchline: Leslie's response — Michigan wolverines eating Ann's toes — is delivered as casual comfort/comeuppance
jokes.explanation: Leslie's dark little comeback is slightly out of character but amusing. 'Eat your toes' is specific enough to be funny rather than generic.

jokes.text: April: 'I love you too.' / April: 'I-I couldn't—I couldn't quite hear you.' / Leslie: 'My going-away present to you will be that I do not make you audibly say that you love me.'
jokes.setup: Leslie says she loves April and asks April to say she loves her back
jokes.punchline: April says it inaudibly; Leslie tortures her by pretending she can't hear; then mercifully releases her with the 'going-away present' framing
jokes.explanation: This is one of the episode's best moments — comedy and emotion perfectly fused. April saying 'I love you too' so quietly it can't be heard is perfect April: she DOES say it but can't bear to. Leslie playing coy ('couldn't quite hear you') is comedic cruelty done with love. The resolution — Leslie's going-away present is sparing April the audible declaration — is structurally brilliant and deeply character-appropriate for both. Extremely high character integration for both.

jokes.text: Chris's morning run: 'I call it my beat the sun run. It's a race between me and the sun.'
jokes.setup: The group arrives at Chris and Ann's door early in the morning; Chris opens it already in running gear
jokes.punchline: Chris has named his morning run and framed it as a personal competition with the sun — his positivity applied to astronomy
jokes.explanation: Classic Chris — he has named a competition against a celestial body and treats it with total sincerity. 'It's a race between me and the sun' is a great explanatory line that makes it worse/better. High character integration.

jokes.text: Ron's handmade box: 'Quarter-sawn zebra wood adjoined by floating tenons to the black walnut corner posts. Finished with a wiping varnish that's a secret Swanson family recipe. Handmade at my woodshop, and you are correct. It is gorgeous.'
jokes.setup: The group presents Ron's handmade box as their gift for Chris
jokes.punchline: Ron delivers the woodworking specs with the reverence of a sommelier — and then preemptively confirms Chris's response ('you are correct, it is gorgeous') before Chris can speak
jokes.explanation: Ron describing his woodwork is always a comedic goldmine — the precise terminology delivered with complete earnestness. 'You are correct. It is gorgeous.' is the ideal button: Ron doesn't wait for the compliment, he provides it himself because it's simply true. Peak Ron character comedy.

jokes.text: 'Wait a minute, who's G-J-L-G-G?' / 'That's Garry Jerry Larry Gergich Gengurch. I burned in all my names. I really — I didn't know what to do.'
jokes.setup: Everyone has burned their initials into the box; one set of initials is puzzling
jokes.punchline: Jerry has burned in all his names — Garry, Jerry, Larry, Gergich, Gengurch — because he genuinely doesn't know which is correct. 'I didn't know what to do.'
jokes.explanation: Great callback to the show's long-running 'what is Jerry's name' gag, but elevated because Jerry has internalized the confusion — he doesn't know which name is correct either. 'I really — I didn't know what to do' is the perfect helpless delivery. The inclusion of 'Gengurch' (a misspelling) is an extra touch.

jokes.text: Ron: 'Salt water will warp the wood. So keep your tears in your eyes where they belong.'
jokes.setup: Chris is visibly emotional, a tear threatening to fall
jokes.punchline: Ron interrupts the emotional moment with a practical woodworking concern — 'keep your tears in your eyes where they belong' — delivered as genuine advice
jokes.explanation: The best joke in the episode. 'Salt water will warp the wood. So keep your tears in your eyes where they belong.' is a near-perfect construction. First beat: practical concern for the handmade gift (salt water + wood = real problem). Second beat: the extension of that logic to an anti-emotion instruction that is somehow the most Ron thing imaginable. 'Where they belong' as the capper is genius — it implies tears have a designated location (inside your eyes) and leaving that location is improper. It's also somehow both funny AND a Ron-style expression of emotion (he cares enough about the gift to protect it). Exceptional originality, structure, economy, character integration, and earned quality. Comparable to the Swanson-pyramid-of-greatness tier of Ron jokes.

jokes.text: Ann asks if she can still call Ron to discuss Jennifer Aniston's future; Ron: 'Not if I call you first.'
jokes.setup: Ann and Ron are saying goodbye; she asks if they can maintain their friendship through phone calls about celebrity gossip
jokes.punchline: Ron doesn't refuse — he one-ups her, implying he cares MORE about Jennifer Aniston's future than she does
jokes.explanation: Exceptional Ron joke. The misdirection is perfect: we expect Ron to reject celebrity gossip as beneath him (entirely in character). Instead he reverses — 'not if I call you first' — revealing a hidden vulnerability: Ron Swanson secretly cares about Jennifer Aniston. The joke works on three levels: (1) the surprise reversal, (2) the implication that Ron is sitting at home waiting to discuss Jennifer Aniston, (3) his competitive framing (of course Ron would frame caring about someone as a competition he intends to win). Second-best joke in the episode.

jokes.text: Leslie: 'But most importantly, you taught me that I can't pull off a tulip skirt.' Ann: 'It's just not your shape.'
jokes.setup: Leslie is delivering a heartfelt summary of everything Ann taught her — patience, balance, bureaucratic courage
jokes.punchline: After a series of meaningful life lessons, the 'most important' thing is fashion advice: Leslie can't pull off a tulip skirt. And Ann confirms it bluntly.
jokes.explanation: Excellent structural joke — the escalating list of meaningful lessons ('balance,' 'patience,' 'bureaucratic caution') makes the final item ('tulip skirt') a perfect anti-climax/misdirection. And Ann's flat 'It's just not your shape' — practical, honest, and slightly brutal — is the ideal button. The friendship is encapsulated in Ann's willingness to be this direct about fashion.

jokes.text: Leslie: 'Either he flaked or he tripped and impaled himself on his own giant scissors.'
jokes.setup: The ceremonial ribbon-cutting person hasn't shown up
jokes.punchline: Leslie's two theories: (1) he flaked, (2) he impaled himself on the giant ceremonial scissors — presented as equally plausible
jokes.explanation: Good dark joke — the image of a ribbon-cutting specialist impaled on ceremonial scissors is absurd and specific. 'His own giant scissors' is the right phrasing. Leslie treating both options as equivalently valid is the character touch.

jokes.text: Ann: 'All right, I got my park. That's all I wanted from you. Friendship over.'
jokes.setup: The groundbreaking has just happened — a genuine, emotional fulfillment of Leslie and Ann's five-year friendship promise
jokes.punchline: Ann immediately declares the friendship over now that she has what she wanted — a dark joke that also clearly isn't true
jokes.explanation: Good deflation beat after an emotional moment. 'Friendship over' as a button is economical and funny. Works as a tonal reset.

jokes.text: Leslie's farewell to Chris: '...I thought there was no man on earth good enough for Ann Perkins. And I still think that. But if there is no one actually good enough for her, you are pretty damn close.'
jokes.setup: Leslie is delivering a heartfelt farewell to Chris
jokes.punchline: The compliment contains an insult in its structure — 'no man is good enough for Ann' is maintained, but Chris gets credit for being the least-bad option
jokes.explanation: Well-constructed backhanded compliment that is actually a sincere expression of Leslie's worldview. The logic is internally consistent: no one is good enough → Chris is the closest → that IS the compliment. Good Leslie characterization.

jokes.text: 'There's a lot of Sarah McLachlan, so, Chris, I apologize. Things are gonna get emotional.'
jokes.setup: Leslie has packed sandwiches and a mix CD for Ann and Chris's drive
jokes.punchline: The apology is specifically to Chris — because Leslie knows the Sarah McLachlan will overwhelm his emotions specifically (his known tendency to cry)
jokes.explanation: Good character joke — Chris's emotional sensitivity is well-established, and Sarah McLachlan is the culturally perfect choice of music to weaponize that. The preemptive apology is thoughtful in a comedic way.

jokes.text: Ron arrives at the diner: 'Breakfast, Knope?' / Leslie: 'There has never been a sadness that can't be cured by breakfast food.'
jokes.setup: Leslie is standing alone after Ann and Chris drive away, visibly devastated
jokes.punchline: Ron appears with a single-word invitation to breakfast — and Leslie's response is a Knope-ism that also happens to be true
jokes.explanation: A warm comedic beat that also works emotionally. 'There has never been a sadness that can't be cured by breakfast food' is very Leslie — a sweeping declarative statement about a mundane thing. Ron's economical one-word invitation ('Breakfast, Knope?') is perfect Ron. The friendship between them is expressed entirely in these two lines.

jokes.text: Tom: 'I call sitting on your lap.' / Ben: 'You can't — I — double shotgun! We call double shotgun! How come people don't do that more often?' / Ron: 'It's illegal.'
jokes.setup: The shotgun competition escalates as everyone tries to claim a front-seat position
jokes.punchline: Ben invents 'double shotgun' with total enthusiasm; Ron's dry explanation that it's illegal deflates the entire thing
jokes.explanation: Great three-character escalation. Tom's 'sitting on your lap' escalates the absurdity; Ben's 'double shotgun' invention and his genuine 'how come people don't do that more often?' shows his excitement; Ron's flat 'It's illegal' is the perfect grounding button. Each character is exactly themselves.

jokes.text: 'How come people don't do that more often?' / 'It's illegal.'
jokes.setup: April has called double shotgun and the car is overloaded
jokes.punchline: Someone asks why people don't do this more often (pile in); the dry response: 'It's illegal.'
jokes.explanation: A brief button joke that gets a light laugh. The structure is simple (innocent question / deflating answer) and it works adequately. Low character integration since we can't attribute it. Doesn't reach above average.

jokes.text: Final scene: raise your hand for waffles / bacon and eggs / the group chaos as they head to the diner
jokes.setup: The group is heading to breakfast together; someone asks for orders
jokes.punchline: The overlapping, enthusiastic breakfast orders — including Jerry, hands raised — is a warm comedic button suggesting life goes on
jokes.explanation: Functional warm-closing beat. Not a big joke but a nice comedic note to end on. The laughter is more relief than punchline.

tmdb_overview: Ben attempts to surprise Leslie with a special anniversary gift. Tom and Adam try to help Leslie bring positive light to the Pawnee-Eagleton merger, while April asserts her new authority as Donna's boss.
insight: Ann and Chris's departure fuels 54 jokes in 42 minutes—character comedy dominates their exit episode.
